---
title: "Glossary"
---

A musical term earns its keep when it helps you hear something or build
something. So every entry below points back to the lesson where the word first
does real work. The definitions tell you how this book uses each term and
recover the idea underneath it. They don't replace the lesson, which is where
the sound, the code, and the argument live.

### Accent

Extra weight on one event, put there by amplitude, timing, register, or timbre.
Meter only becomes audible through a repeating pattern of accents. Lessons 13
and 36.

### Accidental

A sharp, flat, or natural written beside a note. In this book's notation model
it changes every later occurrence of the same letter and octave in that voice
until the bar ends. [Lesson 40](../parts/08-reading-notation/40-key-signatures-defaults.qmd).

### ADSR

Attack, decay, sustain, release: the four stages of an envelope. Together they
describe how a sound's amplitude moves while a note is held and after you let
go. [Lesson 7](../parts/01-why-sound-has-structure/07-envelope-instrument.qmd).

### Antecedent

The opening phrase of a question-and-answer pair. It ends with enough
instability that you expect a second phrase to follow. [Lesson 34](../parts/07-melody-phrase-and-form/34-question-answer.qmd).

### Articulation

How a note begins, continues, and ends. Legato and staccato are articulations;
the pitch stays put while the gesture changes. [Lesson 7](../parts/01-why-sound-has-structure/07-envelope-instrument.qmd).

### Bar

One fixed span of metrical time. Bars group beats according to the time
signature, and they give written accidentals their scope. [Lesson 13](../parts/03-rhythm-and-meter/13-bars-accent-that-makes-meter-audible.qmd).

### Beat

Sonic Pi's scheduling unit, and the pulse a listener taps along with. How long
it lasts in seconds depends on the tempo. [Lesson 3](../parts/00-getting-a-sound-out/03-time-beats-seconds.qmd).

### Cadence

A harmonic ending or pause. Authentic, plagal, half, and deceptive cadences
close a phrase to different degrees and in different ways. [Lesson 29](../parts/06-chords-and-harmony/29-cadences-are-punctuation.qmd).

### Chord

Several notes treated as one harmonic event. This book starts with three-note
triads, then splits their notes into independent voices. [Lesson 26](../parts/06-chords-and-harmony/26-triads-stacked-thirds.qmd).

### Chromatic

Using pitches outside the current diatonic scale, or moving by semitones. A
chromatic chord can point briefly at another tonic. Lessons 8 and 52.

### Consonance

Smoothness or stability between sounding pitches. It depends on their frequency
relationship, spectrum, register, and setting, so it isn't a fixed property of
an interval. [Lesson 5](../parts/01-why-sound-has-structure/05-consonance-small-whole-numbers.qmd).

### Contour

Up, down, and repeated motion in a melody, with the exact interval sizes thrown
away. Strip a tune back to its contour and you can often still recognise it.
[Lesson 32](../parts/07-melody-phrase-and-form/32-contour-rhythm-are-separable.qmd).

### Degree

Scale position counted from the tonic. Degree numbers keep a note's job intact
when you move the tune to another key. [Lesson 22](../parts/05-scales-and-keys/22-scale-degrees-pull-toward-home.qmd).

### Dissonance

Roughness or instability between pitches. It can be acoustic, harmonic, or
contextual, and it usually supplies motion; read it as an error and you lose the
reason most music moves at all. [Lesson 5](../parts/01-why-sound-has-structure/05-consonance-small-whole-numbers.qmd).

### Dominant

Scale degree 5 and the chord built on it. The dominant is stable enough to hold
your attention and unstable enough to point at the tonic. [Lesson 22](../parts/05-scales-and-keys/22-scale-degrees-pull-toward-home.qmd).

### Drone

One sustained or repeated pitch held under changing material. Put a drone under
a scale and modal differences get much easier to hear. [Lesson 22](../parts/05-scales-and-keys/22-scale-degrees-pull-toward-home.qmd).

### Duration

How much musical time an event occupies. In the event schema you measure it in
beats, so the tempo can change without touching the score. [Lesson 12](../parts/03-rhythm-and-meter/12-durations-fractions.qmd).

### Enharmonic

Two written names for the same key on an equal-tempered instrument, such as
F-sharp and G-flat. They sound identical and mean different things, because
spelling records harmonic function. [Lesson 10](../parts/02-pitch-space/10-sharps-flats-why-spelling-sound.qmd).

### Envelope

How amplitude, or some other parameter, changes over a sound's lifetime.
Envelope shape carries much of an instrument's identity. [Lesson 7](../parts/01-why-sound-has-structure/07-envelope-instrument.qmd).

### Frequency

Pressure-wave cycles per second, measured in hertz. Double a frequency and you
raise the pitch by one octave. [Lesson 4](../parts/01-why-sound-has-structure/04-one-note-many-notes.qmd).

### Harmony

Notes sounding together, and the motion from one such state to the next. Lessons
26 to 31 turn harmony into chord and voice data.

### Interval

Distance between two pitches, carrying two measurements at once: a diatonic
number such as third, and a chromatic size in semitones. You can't name an
interval from the semitone count alone. [Lesson 18](../parts/04-intervals/18-interval-carries-two-measurements.qmd).

### Inversion

A chord with something other than its root in the bass. Pitch classes stay the
same; what shifts is the chord's balance. [Lesson 27](../parts/06-chords-and-harmony/27-inversions-voicing.qmd).

### Key

Tonal environment organised around one tonic and its scale. A key supplies
defaults, and it never confines the music to seven pitches. [Lesson 21](../parts/05-scales-and-keys/21-major-scale-step-formula.qmd).

### Leading tone

Scale degree 7 when it sits one semitone below the tonic. That single semitone
is where its pull comes from. [Lesson 22](../parts/05-scales-and-keys/22-scale-degrees-pull-toward-home.qmd).

### Meter

Repeating hierarchy of strong and weak beats. A time signature describes the
grid; accents are what make the hierarchy audible. [Lesson 13](../parts/03-rhythm-and-meter/13-bars-accent-that-makes-meter-audible.qmd).

### Mode

A scale pattern heard against its own tonal centre. Rotate the major-scale steps
and you get the seven diatonic modes. [Lesson 24](../parts/05-scales-and-keys/24-modes-over-drone.qmd).

### Motive

A short musical idea that stays recognisable through controlled change. Pitch,
rhythm, contour, and articulation can each carry part of its identity. [Lesson 33](../parts/07-melody-phrase-and-form/33-motive-sequence-development.qmd).

### Octave

Interval between two pitches whose frequencies stand in a 2:1 ratio. In
MIDI-style numbering it spans twelve semitones. [Lesson 9](../parts/02-pitch-space/09-octaves-address-space.qmd).

### Pitch class

All octave copies of one chromatic pitch, treated as a single class. For integer
notes, `note % 12` hands it to you. [Lesson 8](../parts/02-pitch-space/08-twelve-pitch-classes.qmd).

### Phrase

A musical unit you hear as one gesture, often ending in a cadence. Phrases pair
up as question and answer. [Lesson 34](../parts/07-melody-phrase-and-form/34-question-answer.qmd).

### Register

High, middle, or low region a pitch or a voice occupies. Register decides
weight, clarity, and how much room the other parts have. [Lesson 9](../parts/02-pitch-space/09-octaves-address-space.qmd).

### Rest

A measured span in which a voice attacks nothing. It still occupies time in the
score, and that's what separates it from silence you forgot to write. [Lesson 14](../parts/03-rhythm-and-meter/14-rests-dots-ties.qmd).

### Rhythm

Pattern of onsets and durations against a pulse. Change every pitch in a tune
and the rhythm alone can keep it recognisable. [Lesson 12](../parts/03-rhythm-and-meter/12-durations-fractions.qmd).

### Scale

An ordered pitch collection tied to a tonal reference. Step formulas generate
scales, so you don't store a separate note list for every root. [Lesson 21](../parts/05-scales-and-keys/21-major-scale-step-formula.qmd).

### Semitone

One step in the twelve-part equal-tempered octave, and one integer step in Sonic
Pi pitch arithmetic. [Lesson 6](../parts/01-why-sound-has-structure/06-twelve-notes-one-compromise.qmd).

### Syncopation

An onset or continuation that pulls weight away from the positions the meter
leads you to expect. [Lesson 15](../parts/03-rhythm-and-meter/15-syncopation-grid.qmd).

### Tempo

Rate of the beat, normally given in beats per minute. Change it and seconds per
beat change with it, while your score durations stay exactly as written.
[Lesson 3](../parts/00-getting-a-sound-out/03-time-beats-seconds.qmd).

### Timbre

Spectral and temporal character that tells two sounds apart at the same pitch
and loudness. Harmonics and envelopes both feed into it. Lessons 4 and 7.

### Tonic

The pitch and chord you hear as home in a key or mode. Every other degree is
understood through its relation to that one. [Lesson 22](../parts/05-scales-and-keys/22-scale-degrees-pull-toward-home.qmd).

### Triad

A three-note chord built from a root and two stacked thirds. Major, minor,
diminished, and augmented triads differ in the sizes of those thirds. [Lesson 26](../parts/06-chords-and-harmony/26-triads-stacked-thirds.qmd).

### Tuplet

A division that fits an unusual number of equal events into a standard span,
such as three notes in the time normally taken by two. [Lesson 17](../parts/03-rhythm-and-meter/17-tuplets-3-against-2.qmd).

### Voice leading

Motion of individual lines from one harmony to the next. Small moves and
retained common tones are what make a progression sound connected. [Lesson 31](../parts/06-chords-and-harmony/31-voice-leading-optimisation-problem.qmd).

### Voicing

Octaves, spacing, order, and doubling you choose for a chord's pitches. One
chord supports many voicings, and they don't sound alike. [Lesson 27](../parts/06-chords-and-harmony/27-inversions-voicing.qmd).
